# What You Need to Know About Sports Psychiatry: An Introductory Curriculum for Psychiatry Residents

**Authors:** Jowan Watson; Marie Desir; Claire Twark; Hermioni L. Amonoo

**Affiliations:** 1 Medical Student, Harvard Medical School, and Psychiatry Resident, Department of Psychiatry, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School | 2 Psychiatry Resident, Department of Psychiatry, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School | 3 Instructor in Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School | 4 Associate Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Harvard Medical School

## Abstract

Sports psychiatry is a growing subspecialty focusing on the psychiatric care of athletes. However, efforts to increase sports psychiatry training in residency are lacking.

A 120-minute introductory curriculum for the Brigham and Women's Hospital/Harvard Medical School Psychiatry Residency Program was developed and tested for feasibility. Kern's curriculum design and a literature review on sports psychiatry topics, including a review of the International Society for Sports Psychiatry curriculum for trainees, guided development. Pre- and postassessments were used to assess acceptability and impact on resident learners. Residents provided qualitative feedback on how to improve the curriculum.

Thirty-five of 56 residents received the training. Eighteen of 35 residents (51.4%) completed the surveys. Residents had minimal baseline knowledge in sports psychiatry, and this introduction enhanced their objective knowledge scores (mean 0.67 vs 0.93; mean difference = 0.26, 95% CI, 0.16–0.43; P < .001; Cohen d = 1.56), subjective confidence (mean 1.56 vs 3.22; mean difference = 1.65, 95% CI, 1.31–2.00; P < .001; Cohen d = 3.13), and subjective knowledge (mean 1.67 vs 3.40; mean difference = 1.73, 95% CI, 1.42–2.05; P < .001; Cohen d = 3.22). Residents’ qualitative feedback suggested allocating more time and a broader scope for curriculum improvement.

Implementing an introductory sports psychiatry curriculum in psychiatric training is feasible and enhances residents’ knowledge and confidence in sports psychiatry topics. More work is needed to explore the best ways of increasing opportunities for sports psychiatry training in graduate medical education programs.

## Educational Objectives

By the end of this activity, the learner will be able to: 1.Explain sports psychiatry and the clinical role of a sports psychiatrist in caring for athletes.2.Identify psychiatric conditions and behaviors that are more prevalent in athlete populations.3.Construct a biopsychosocial formulation for an athlete patient that incorporates developmental and psychological factors.4.Differentiate disordered eating, eating disorders, relative energy deficiency in sport, and the Female Athlete Triad in terms of their diagnostic features and clinical implications.5.Outline the process of obtaining a therapeutic use exemption for an athlete, integrating knowledge of prohibited and preferred psychiatric medication options.

## Introduction

Within the last decade, suicide has increased from the fourth to the second leading cause of death for National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) athletes.1,2 Nearly 45% of elite athletes report significant depressive and anxiety symptoms, with prospective studies finding that 5%-35% experience mental health disorders over a 12-month period.3 Although the NCAA has prioritized athlete mental health,4 a shortage of clinicians specialized in sports psychiatry persists, and consistent training opportunities for psychiatry trainees are lacking.5,6

Since 2018, the International Society for Sports Psychiatry (ISSP) has provided an online curriculum that includes literature reviews, mentorship, and scholarly engagement to enhance training. The ISSP's certification of additional training is the only formalized sports psychiatry training for psychiatry trainees in the United States, as there is no Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME)-accredited board certification available.7

Existing training opportunities, such as the ISSP online curriculum and longitudinal electives in Canada and Germany, provide in-depth experiences for motivated trainees but are often elective, time intensive, and dependent on local expertise.5,8–10 Given the success of structured curricula in other subspecialties, such as geriatric, addiction, and consult-liaison psychiatry, a standardized introductory sports psychiatry curriculum should be developed.11–13 Hence, we developed and piloted a 120-minute introductory sports psychiatry curriculum for adult psychiatry residents, grounded in Kern's curriculum development framework and informed by adult learning principles (Appendix A). Our primary goals (listed in educational objectives) were to assess feasibility and to evaluate changes in residents’ objective knowledge, subjective knowledge, and confidence in foundational sports psychiatry topics.

## Methods

### Participants

In July 2024, the residency training director was presented with the proposed study and provided approval to offer the didactic session. All residents from the Brigham and Women's Hospital/Harvard Medical School Psychiatry Residency Program who received the didactic curriculum during their scheduled didactics on November 14, 2024, were included as participants. The residency assistant administrator emailed all residents at least 1 week before the scheduled session. Residents received details about the session and were given the opportunity to voluntarily participate in the pre- and postassessments before the scheduled didactic. To promote anonymity in assessments, residents were given a nonidentifiable identification code for assessment completion. Appendix B includes the pre- and postsurvey questions, and Appendices A, C, and D help guide the implementation of this curriculum. Appendix D is a facilitator's guide that walks through everything in the module in detail to help users with the implementation. The Harvard University Office of Regulatory Affairs and Research Compliance provided an exemption from review (IRB24-1255).

### Curriculum Development

#### Theoretical frameworks for curricula design

We adopted Thomas and Kern's framework for curriculum development, which integrates structured progression with adaptability.14 Kern's framework follows 6 steps, including problem identification, a targeted needs assessment, goals and objectives development, educational strategies selection, implementation of the curriculum, and evaluation and assessment. For this study, we executed steps 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 of Kern's steps for curriculum design in medical education. A rationale statement and needs assessment (step 1) was conducted via literature review (Jowan Watson), which revealed limited data on sports psychiatry curricula for psychiatry residency training. A targeted needs assessment (step 2) was not done due to time constraints and because of the pilot nature of the study. Instead, for step 2, we conducted content prioritization (Jowan Watson and Claire Twark). Goals and objectives (step 3) were developed in accordance with ACGME milestones for psychiatry residencies (Jowan Watson and Claire Twark),10 and educational strategies (step 4), implementation (step 5), and evaluation (step 6) were conducted and are detailed next.

To determine and prioritize curricular content, from March to October 2024, Jowan Watson reviewed the literature to identify salient topics within sports psychiatry that psychiatry residents must know as trainees. The literature review also included a review of the ISSP curriculum for trainees.15 Literature was condensed into the most relevant topics for resident psychiatrists and reviewed by an experienced sports psychiatrist (Claire Twark). Through peer review and author consensus (Jowan Watson and Claire Twark), goals and objectives informed by the ACGME competencies for psychiatry were developed. The overarching topics of “Defining sports psychiatry,” “Biopsychosocial formulation and substance use in athletes,” “Eating disorders and RED-S,” “Medication preferences for sports psychiatrists,” and “How to do a therapeutic use exemption” were included in the final curriculum delivered by 2 facilitators: Jowan Watson was the lead facilitator and attended in-person, and Claire Twark was an additional facilitator and attended via Zoom. Details of the curriculum using our adaptation of Kern's steps (excluding rationale statement, goals and objectives, and teaching strategies, which are described earlier) for curriculum design are outlined in the Figure.14

*Figure.: Curriculum design in accordance with Thomas and Kern's 6 steps for curriculum design.*

#### Content prioritization

A literature review conducted by Jowan Watson, including the ISSP curriculum for trainees, provided a comprehensive framework for curricula competencies. Peer review and author consensus between Jowan Watson and Claire Twark condensed the literature review into the most salient topics for resident trainees to learn during the comprehensive introductory curriculum (see the Figure and Appendix B). Importantly, these topics were considered most salient for an introduction to sports psychiatry for resident trainees, enhancing their knowledge in aspects of sports psychiatry even if they choose not to receive additional training in sports psychiatry.

#### Implementation

The curriculum was structured into four 30-minute didactic sessions, totaling 120 minutes (see Appendices B and D). Topics covered included an overview of the field of sports psychiatry, exploration of the biopsychosocial formulation of athletes and their psychological risk factors for substance use, disordered eating in athletes, psychopharmacology preferences for athletes, and how to do a therapeutic use exemption.

### Evaluation and Assessment

We modeled pre- and posttest assessments (see Appendix C) after survey questions used to evaluate similar curricula for medical trainees.16,17 Content areas evaluated by the assessments include biopsychosocial formulation for athletes, substance use in athletes, banned substances in sports, therapeutic use exemptions, disordered eating and relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S), and medication preferences for psychiatric disorders in athletes. Objective knowledge was assessed by fact-based questions with 1 correct answer based on the material covered in the session. We also assessed subjective knowledge and confidence in their ability to define sports psychiatry and the role of a sports psychiatrist, identify medications banned in and out of competition, and obtain a therapeutic use exemption for an athlete.

Additionally, the posttest assessment included 3 open-ended questions for general feedback about the didactic session and suggestions for improvement.

### Survey Distribution and Data Collection

Participants completed the assessment on November 14, 2024, via a Qualtrics survey. Participants were verbally given the option to voluntarily participate in the pre- and postassessments.

### Data Analysis

We used descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, and proportions) to characterize the sample and survey responses. For each domain (objective knowledge, subjective confidence, and subjective knowledge), we conducted paired 2-sample t tests to compare pre- and postsession scores, calculated mean differences and 95% confidence intervals based on the t distribution, and quantified effect sizes using the Cohen d for paired samples.18 Assumptions for paired t tests (continuous outcome, matched pairs, and independence) were satisfied by design. We examined histograms, Q-Q plots, and boxplots of the pre-post difference scores to assess normality and outliers and conducted Shapiro-Wilk tests, which did not show evidence of substantial departures from normality. Analyses were conducted using Microsoft Excel (version 365; Microsoft Corporation). Statistical significance was defined as a 2-sided alpha level of .05.

For qualitative data, we used a thematic analysis informed by the phenomenological approach of Van Manen.19 Two coders (Jowan Watson and Marie Desir) independently reviewed responses, identified preliminary codes, and met to reconcile discrepancies and develop final themes by consensus.

## Results

### Quantitative Results

Of 35 participating residents, 18 (51.4%) completed both surveys and were included in the analysis. While 20 and 22 residents completed the pre- and postsession surveys, respectively, only paired responses (ie, from 18 residents) were analyzed. Seventy-two percent responded that they felt confident/very confident in their ability to explain the role of a sports psychiatrist postsession (Table 1). Sixty-one percent responded that they felt knowledgeable/very knowledgeable about formulating a patient who identifies as a current/former athlete postsession (see Table 1). Overall, the pre- and posttest survey responses indicate increased resident knowledge and confidence in sports psychiatry topics (see Table 1). All effect sizes are considered large.18

*Table 1. Pre- and Posttest Assessment of Sports Psychiatry Curriculum-Related Confidence and Knowledge (N = 18), Measures Individual Descriptive Statistics*

#### Objective knowledge

The average pretest objective knowledge score was 0.67 out of 1.0 (SD = 0.21), and the average posttest objective knowledge score was 0.93 out of 1.0 (SD = 0.12). All assumptions for a paired t test were checked and met. We found a significant increase in objective knowledge scores between pre- and posttest assessments, t(17) = 5.6, P < .001. The mean difference was 0.26 (95% CI, 0.16–0.43), with a large effect size (Cohen d = 1.56) (see Table 1).

#### Subjective confidence

The average pretest subjective confidence score was 1.56 (SD = 0.60), and the average posttest subjective confidence score was 3.22 (SD = 0.47). All assumptions for a paired t test were checked and met. We found a significant difference between pre- and posttest subjective confidence scores, t(17) = 10.3, P < .001, with a mean difference of 1.65 (95% CI, 1.31–2.0) and a large effect size (Cohen d = 3.13) (see Table 1). Residents showed increased confidence, with many shifting from “not confident” to “confident/very confident” after the session. For example, being confident or very confident in explaining the role of a sports psychiatrist increased from 17% to 72%, and confidence in discussing and caring for most aspects of psychiatric care for current/former athletes rose from 0% to 44%, with similar improvements for obtaining a therapeutic use exemption, identifying banned medications, and managing disordered eating and RED-S.

#### Subjective knowledge

The average pretest subjective knowledge score was 1.67 (SD = 0.58), and the average posttest subjective knowledge score was 3.40 (SD = 0.49). We found a significant increase between pre- and posttest subjective knowledge scores, t(17) = 11.5, P < .001, with a mean difference of 1.73 (95% CI, 1.42–2.05) and a very large effect size (Cohen d = 3.22) (see Table 1). Item-level analyses of subjective knowledge showed improvement, with residents moving from predominantly “not knowledgeable” to “knowledgeable/very knowledgeable” on core sports psychiatry topics. For instance, being knowledgeable or very knowledgeable about formulating a patient who identifies as a current/former athlete rose from 6% to 61%, and similar shifts were observed for understanding psychological conflicts in athletes versus non-athletes, substance misuse and suicide rates, World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) banned substances and therapeutic use exemptions, disordered eating and RED-S, and preferred medications for psychiatric disorders in athletes.

### Qualitative Results

Survey participants were asked 3 open-ended questions in the posttest survey. The first question asked the trainees to identify 1 thing they enjoyed most about this session. From their responses, we identified the themes of engagement and interactivity, practical takeaways and application, the speaker's delivery and effectiveness, and an evidence-based focus (Table 2). Specific comments included “Audience engagement and clear show of passion for the topic from the speaker” and “Interactive presentation - lot of opportunities to discuss with others” (see Table 2).

*Table 2. Themes Identified From Participant Comments and Feedback About the Workshop Using Van Manen's (1990) Approach to Extracting Specific Phrases or Sentences*

The second question asked the trainees to identify 2 ways to improve the session. The themes identified from this question were the allocation of more time for content and practical application, more breaks and rest periods, more interactivity and personal engagement, and additional resources. Specific comments included “spending more time looking at case examples,” “more patient vignettes,” “decreasing the amount of content per unit time,” and “more and longer breaks” (see Table 2).

When asked to identify 2 things they wished they had learned during this session, participants described expanding the scope and coverage, pharmacological considerations, mental health in special populations, and treatment approaches and therapy. Specific comments included “are E-sports included in sports psychiatry,” “how to help former athletes develop identities outside of sports,” “more information on regulations,” “post-athletic career outcomes,” “side effects to be aware of,” “symptoms associated with CTE [chronic traumatic encephalopathy] and appropriate workup,” “salient differences among different sports and implications for mental health,” “unique considerations for transgender athletes and retired athletes,” “types of therapy best to offer athletes,” and “further discussion of pharmacotherapy considerations” (see Table 2).

## Discussion

Interest in sports psychiatry has grown substantially, yet formal training remains limited in adult psychiatry residency programs. We successfully developed and implemented an introductory sports psychiatry curriculum for psychiatry residents at an academic medical center, demonstrating increased resident knowledge and confidence in sports psychiatry topics. Residents also provided feedback related to curriculum improvement, including the addition of more case vignettes.

A key strength of our curriculum was the incorporation of role-playing, small-group discussions, and case-based learning to promote learner engagement. Similar approaches have been effective in other areas of psychiatric education. For example, Ross and Rohrbaugh20 implemented a neuroscience curriculum that significantly improved resident assessment performance and interest in neuroscience through case- and group-based discussions. Further, a pilot cultural sensitivity workshop for psychiatry residents by LoboPrabhu and colleagues21 employed role-play strategies and demonstrated significant posttest knowledge improvements (F = 30.6; P < .001). Additionally, Kavanagh and colleagues22 found that a group discussion-based psychopharmacology prescribing workshop improved psychiatry residents’ comfort with prescribing (P < .05). These findings convey that active-learning approaches warrant further investigation as strategies for implementing sports psychiatry training during residency.

Unlike the ISSP online curriculum,15 which emphasizes self-directed learning, mentorship, and certification for trainees who seek additional specialization, our curriculum is designed as a brief introductory session embedded within core residency didactics. Similarly, compared with the multiweek or multihour clinical curricula described in Canada and Germany, our 120-minute session requires substantially fewer resources and does not depend on residents’ ability to schedule elective rotations. This design makes foundational sports psychiatry content accessible to all residents, including those who may not ultimately pursue dedicated sports psychiatry rotations.8,9

Several practical lessons emerged from our implementation of this introductory curriculum. First, our use of Kern's framework for curriculum design ensured evidence-based content prioritization and effective teaching techniques, thereby aiding improvements in resident knowledge and confidence. Prior to the session, participants had minimal knowledge of sports psychiatry foundational topics, with pretest objective knowledge scores of 67%, and the very large effect sizes in this study suggest that this curriculum significantly enhanced their knowledge and confidence within sports psychiatry. Residents provided valuable feedback for improving the curriculum, including requests for more case vignettes, longer sessions, and additional breaks. For example, additional patient vignettes would enhance residents’ clinical application of sports psychiatry principles. Increasing session duration time, with additional breaks, could improve engagement and retention of information. Second, presession reading can improve learning, allowing trainees to engage in more advanced discussion. Prereading assignments, however, can influence pretest survey responses, a consideration for future research design.

We also identified broader curricular implications for sports psychiatry training at the program level. First, incorporation of the American Association of Directors of Psychiatric Residency Training model curriculum should be explored.23 Second, curriculum implementation in different teaching environments (eg, academic medical centers, community programs) would add to validity and generalizability and ascertain its efficacy for improving resident knowledge and sports psychiatry confidence of the topics. Third, considering continued faculty shortages knowledgeable in sports psychiatry, additional growth is needed in best practices in training non-specialty trained faculty to teach the curriculum. Finally, collaborations with sports medicine societies, universities, and other residency programs may result in broader acceptance and adoption.

### Limitations

This study has several limitations. Response bias may have been present, as trainees previously interested in sports psychiatry may have been more likely to fill out the surveys, underscoring the need for a larger sample size in future studies. Although our curriculum was not informed by a targeted needs assessment as suggested by the Kern model, a comprehensive assessment of resident and training director perspectives of specific deficits in the curriculum could further inform the development of future iterations of this curriculum. Apart from this, we did not control for differences in baseline knowledge. Future studies can address this through more rigorous participant randomization techniques. The literature on sports psychiatry topics is vast and may have introduced selection bias in the content included in our curriculum. Nevertheless, efforts to reduce potential bias were attempted through literature review and peer consensus. Long-term retention was not assessed in this study, as posttest surveys were collected immediately following the session. Future studies should conduct postassessments at different follow-up times, as seen in similar studies.20,22 Implementing 4 didactic segments with multiple active learning strategies within a single 120-minute session was feasible but intensive. Residents’ feedback suggested additional time for case discussion and breaks, underscoring the high cognitive load of the curriculum. Future iterations may benefit from distributing content into shorter sessions or integrating it into a spiral curriculum, aligning with cognitive load theory and the principles of spaced repetition, but these strategies extend beyond the scope of this introductory curriculum. Lastly, the expertise of the facilitators may have influenced curriculum effectiveness; as such, standardized training in conducting this sports psychiatry introductory session is imperative to ensure consistency in its delivery.

### Conclusions and Suggestions for Future Work

Our findings demonstrate that an introductory sports psychiatry curriculum enhances psychiatry resident trainees’ knowledge and confidence in foundational sports psychiatry topics. Psychiatry residents in our sample had minimal baseline knowledge in sports psychiatry, and this introductory session significantly enhanced their knowledge as shown through very large effect sizes for all measures. The demand for sports psychiatrists continues to grow; as such, early exposure in sports psychiatry may encourage further specialization among psychiatry residents. This study demonstrates that it is feasible to conduct a 1-time didactic session in sports psychiatry into psychiatry residency training programs. Future iterations of this intervention will be given to first-year residents, and more advanced sessions tailored to the needs of senior residents are in development.
